claim_or_approach: GitHub Sponsors pays maintainers via a payouts dashboard where maintainers add bank details, or route payouts through a fiscal host, with a Stripe Connect option for receipts.
source_title: Managing your payouts from GitHub Sponsors
support_quote: You can view and manage your payouts from GitHub Sponsors. If you use a fiscal host to receive payouts, you can view your current payout and next estimated payout.
paraphrase: Maintainers manage payouts in a GitHub Sponsors dashboard and can add bank information there; fiscal-host users can see current and estimated payouts but must contact support to change payout details. The page refers payout timing to separate Additional Terms and states no fees.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Requires a payout account (bank or fiscal host) set up by the maintainer
Fiscal-host route trades direct control for a fiscal host's administration
counterevidence: Page does not state payout schedule or fees; those are in Additional Terms not reviewed
uncertainty: Payout timing and fee terms not verified; the page is official documentation but the fee-free claim is from a separate GitHub blog snippet.

claim_or_approach: Open Collective fiscal hosts set their own fees to collectives, commonly 0%-10%, and 15% of host fees go to the Open Collective platform.
support_quote: 15% of Host Fees charged by Fiscal Hosts goes to the platform.
paraphrase: Open Collective documentation says host fees vary by fiscal host, commonly 0% to 10%, and that the platform takes 15% of those host fees; the example given is a 10% fee on $1,000 yielding $100 host fees with $15 to the platform.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Money reaches maintainers net of host fee plus payment processing fees
Host fee level depends on which fiscal host a project joins
counterevidence: Some hosts charge more than 10% or add processing and service fees (per third-party guides and a FOSS resource)
uncertainty: The page does not explicitly state who sets fees; inferred from the variation. Rates may have changed since the page was captured.

claim_or_approach: Open Source Collective, the fiscal host serving most open source projects on Open Collective, charges 10% of funds raised, which covers accounting, payments, tax reporting, invoices and legal liability.
paraphrase: Open Source Collective's application page lists a 10% fee on funds raised; the page says this covers operating costs such as accounting, payments, tax reporting, invoices and legal liability.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Fee is taken from gross donations before they reach maintainers
In exchange, project gets legal, tax and payment administration
counterevidence: Fee split into two 5% parts in a 2021 update, total unchanged (search snippet)
uncertainty: Fee could have changed after capture; the quoted line is from the fetched application page.

claim_or_approach: The Open Source Pledge asks companies to pay at least $2,000 per full-time developer per year to open source maintainers and/or foundations of their choosing, with the pledge itself not handling funds.
support_quote: a minimum of $2000 per year per full-time equivalent developer
paraphrase: Companies commit to a minimum of $2,000 per year per full-time-equivalent developer, paid to maintainers or foundations they choose; the pledge does not hold money, so payments go directly to recipients. Members self-report payments.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Voluntary; depends on company participation and self-reporting
Money goes direct, so no intermediary fee but no pooled oversight
counterevidence: Commentary questions whether the $2000 figure fits all regions and whether paying for vendor subscriptions counts (LWN, blog posts snippets)
Search snippets report a ddev campaign that raised about $10,038
uncertainty: Member totals and actual dollars paid not verified; figures are the pledge's stated terms.

claim_or_approach: NumFOCUS offers fiscal sponsorship (tax-deductible donations, managed funding) and grant programs such as Small Development Grants, which sponsored projects can apply for three times a year, plus eligibility for Google Summer of Code.
support_quote: Fiscal sponsorship helps projects attract and manage funding. Donations to NumFOCUS fiscally sponsored projects are tax-deductible.
paraphrase: NumFOCUS fiscally sponsors scientific open source projects so donations are tax-deductible and managed by NumFOCUS; sponsored and affiliated projects can apply for Small Development Grants up to three calls per year. The page does not explain how donations are transferred to individual projects.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Projects need a fiscal oversight team of 3 or 5 to approve spending (per search snippet)
Affiliation is a lighter alternative where the project stays legally separate
counterevidence: Chan Zuckerberg Initiative grants to six sponsored projects reported via search snippet (not verified on page)
uncertainty: Mechanism for disbursing money to maintainers unverified; grant amounts not on fetched page.

claim_or_approach: The Apache Software Foundation pools most donations into a general fund that covers operating costs and shared infrastructure, and only pre-approved, multi-year targeted sponsorships can direct money to specific projects.
support_quote: Your sponsorship helps the ASF meet these expenses.
paraphrase: ASF sponsorship covers general operating costs; standard donations are not earmarked for specific projects. Project-directed support is possible only through Targeted Sponsorships, which need pre-approval and a minimum three-year commitment and also benefit general operations.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Individual maintainers are not paid directly from ASF donations; funds support infrastructure and operations
Targeted sponsorship requires a long commitment and approval
counterevidence: Anthropic's $1.5M gift reported for infrastructure and security, per news snippets (not verified on ASF site)
uncertainty: Fetched page confirms general-fund structure; no evidence in this packet that any ASF money pays individual maintainers.

claim_or_approach: Liberapay is a recurring-donation platform that takes no cut of donations, funded by donations to its own account, though payment processing fees still apply.
support_quote: Liberapay does not take a cut of payments, the service is funded by the donations to its own account.
paraphrase: Liberapay is a recurring-donation service for people whose work donors appreciate; it takes no commission, is funded by donations made to its own account, and donors still pay payment processing fees.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Recurring donor model; fees limited to payment processing
Not specific to open source; covers creators broadly
counterevidence: Search snippets describe Liberapay as aimed mainly at free software and creators, a usage-scale claim not verified here
uncertainty: Scale of open source funding through Liberapay not measured in this packet.

claim_or_approach: The Sovereign Tech Fund (Germany) runs a Fellowship for Maintainers, a pilot that pays maintainers directly, alongside general investments in open digital infrastructure.
support_quote: This is a pilot that pays maintainers directly. The program aims to address structural issues and support open digital infrastructure in the public interest. The first cohort of six maintainers was announced after about around 100 submissions from open source maintainers around the world.
paraphrase: Sovereign Tech Fund's fellowship pilot pays individual maintainers directly; the first cohort was six maintainers chosen from roughly 100 submissions. The fund also invests in projects and has reported over EUR 23 million invested in 60 technologies by its second anniversary.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Government-funded; competitive applications and fixed cohorts
Pilot scope limits how many maintainers are paid
counterevidence: Redirected page was not fetched, so the quote is search-snippet text, not verified on the live page
Sovereign Tech Standards stipend reports (EUR 4,800 to 5,200 per month, May 2026 close) came from one unverified secondary report
uncertainty: Snippet text; current cohort, amounts and deadlines not verified on the agency site.

claim_or_approach: thanks.dev distributes donations across open source dependency trees (about three levels deep) from users who connect GitHub or GitLab accounts, taking a voluntary tip plus a Stripe processing fee.
source_title: The Register: thanks.dev open source funding
support_quote: thanks.dev distributes donations across open source dependency trees. Its design takes donations via GitHub or GitLab accounts and spreads them across the dependency tree three levels deep.
paraphrase: thanks.dev lets donors send money that is spread across the dependencies of the projects they use, reaching transitive dependencies; the platform funds itself through an optional tip and Stripe processing fees.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Maintainers receive money without asking; allocation is algorithmic, so amounts can be small
Requires donor to link repositories or accounts
counterevidence: A 2025 arXiv paper reports high donation-platform adoption among transitive dependencies (snippet), not evaluated here
uncertainty: Snippet is from a 2023 Register article that is over a year old; the thanks.dev current model and volumes were not checked.

claim_or_approach: GitHub Sponsors reports more than $100 million sent to maintainers and projects, with over 280,000 sponsors across 103 regions, and has been fee-free since 2019 per GitHub.
source_title: Open-source maintainers still work underfunded as sponsorship crosses $100 million
support_quote: Open-source maintainers still work underfunded as sponsorship crosses $100 million
paraphrase: Coverage reports that GitHub Sponsors has passed $100 million in sponsorship to maintainers, with over 280,000 sponsors across 103 regions; the same search results attribute a fee-free claim to GitHub's own blog, which was not fetched.
requirements_and_tradeoffs: Scale shows volume but not distribution; most funds may reach few maintainers
counterevidence: Headline frames maintainers as still underfunded despite the total
uncertainty: Only the headline was seen as a snippet; the 280,000 and 103-region figures came from a secondary search summary, and the fee-free claim is unverified on GitHub's blog.
